title: PaidWhole best-option audit
scope: Read-only review of claude/build-platform (PRs 1 to 4 merged), PR 5 (/home/user/pr5) and PR 6 (/home/user/pr6) against CLAUDE.md, change order 001, reconciliation 001, the PRD and ADRs 0056 to 0062.
summary: I took the 105 proposals that survived an adversarial check against the code, merged the duplicates into 64 upgrades, used the checkers' corrections wherever a proposal was wrong, and kept only what is truly better for accuracy, trust, the user or growth. Eleven are critical: each one puts a wrong number in front of a customer or a payer, or lets patient data into the free screening. Most of them sit in the arithmetic around the pricing engine, not in the engine's core: denied lines counted as underpayments, Medicare sequestration compared against the wrong figure, bundled codes such as 97010 priced as if Medicare pays them, approved packets that keep exporting figures after a correction, and dispute deadlines marked 'verified' without knowing what date they run from. Several fixes (#4, #5, #6, #26, #61) can still go inside PR 5 and PR 6 before they merge, which is the cheapest moment there will be, and the GitHub governance fixes (#12) should land before either branch merges. Thirty-seven upgrades are high (a real user cannot do something important, or a large growth limit) and sixteen are medium. Twelve need an exception to the change order's freeze, and several need you to revisit a ruling or an accepted decision; they are listed under 'Decisions only you can make'. The honest cost is roughly 2,550 to 4,150 added hours, of which roughly 1,100 to 1,900 fall ahead of Gate 1. At the change order's 13 hours a week, Gate 1's July 15, 2027 date cannot hold with this list, so either the build's weekly capacity grows or the gate dates move; that choice is yours.

items.title: Denied lines are counted as contract underpayments
items.current: When a payer denies a line (no authorization, visit limit reached, duplicate, filed late, not covered) it pays zero. The engine still prices the line at its full fee, so the whole fee shows as a shortfall, and triage never reads the payer's reason codes. The line becomes a validated, actionable 'paid below the contract rate' finding, and a packet would present a denial as an underpayment.
items.best: Read every line's adjustment and remark codes and classify them through a versioned rule record, never a model. A line whose zero or reduced payment is explained by a denial keeps its price and trace but never becomes validated, never joins a case, and is reported as its own figure, 'Denied: not a rate variance', by category, with the fix for each (get the authorization, appeal medical necessity, correct and resubmit, bill the primary payer). A partly paid line with a denial code goes to review; a bundling denial on a contract without the NCCI flag goes to the reduction-authority review (#17); a code the release does not know holds the line instead of validating it. Store the remark codes the parser already reads, and widen the denial categories (duplicate, coordination of benefits, not covered). The screening template tells prospects to leave denied lines out of their totals.
items.why: Denials are the most common zero-pay lines in a therapy 835. Today they inflate every audit's actionable headline and every case total, and a packet that calls an authorization denial an underpayment gets rejected whole and makes the payer distrust the next one.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no (it still prices denied lines; only triage changes). Ledger: no. Database: yes, a new practice-scoped table for remark codes and wider denial categories (domain model approval), plus a synthetic rule release loaded through /load-release. Freeze exception: no.
items.lands_in: PR 6d (triage accuracy), before PR 7; template wording in PR 6

items.title: Sequestration is compared against the wrong figure
items.area: Engine steps 4c and 7; Q21; D31; PR 6 owner ruling 2
items.current: Medicare Advantage lines lose 2% to sequestration. The engine's expected amount already has the 2% taken out, but the allowed amount the payer reports on the 835 is normally before sequestration. So a correctly paid line shows as overpaid by about 1.6%, small underpayments flip to overpayments, and every shortfall is understated. The repository's own golden line G01 line 3 is underpaid by 50 cents but recorded as overpaid by 31 cents. Your free-screening ruling compares before sequestration, so the screening and the paid audit disagree on the same rows.
items.best: The engine produces two figures, each rounded once with its unrounded value kept: the expected allowed amount before sequestration, and the amount after it, with sequestration moved to the last adjustment step. The variance compares like with like: an 835 that reports the payer's allowed amount is compared with the before-sequestration figure; a line whose allowed amount is paid plus patient share (every EMR export) is compared with the after figure. Where the 835 lists the 2% on the line, code checks it and flags a mismatch for review without changing any price. New engine version and new runs, with a reviewed golden diff like D001. The insurer-payment figure (#11) reads the after-sequestration figure.
items.why: The error sits on every Medicare Advantage non-contracted line, the product's lead offering: it hides small underpayments and puts an expected amount in the packet that a payer reviewer recomputing '100% of Medicare' will find wrong.
items.changes: Pricing engine: yes (order of adjustments and the variance step). Ledger: no. Database: two new columns on priced lines, filled on new runs only (domain model approval). Freeze exception: yes, plus your ruling on moving sequestration last in PRD 11 step 4.
items.lands_in: PR 6c (engine corrections), before PR 7 and before PR 13

items.title: Bundled and non-payable codes are priced as if Medicare pays them
items.current: The engine prices any Medicare fee-schedule record whatever its status code. 97010 (hot or cold packs) is status B: Medicare bundles it into the visit and never pays it separately, yet it is billed on a large share of PT visits and its listed values come to about $5 to $6. Status I codes such as 97014 price the same way. Every Medicare Advantage visit with 97010 becomes an actionable 'underpayment', and the free screening tells prospects Medicare underpaid them on every visit.
items.best: Price only status A. Every other status stops with the existing reason 'no fee-schedule value' and a named detail: bundled, carrier-priced, not valid for Medicare, not covered, deleted, or conditional (status T, until the specialist rules). A status the engine does not recognize also stops. Screens and the screening explain these rows ('Medicare bundles this code into the visit'). If the specialist finds a contract that pays a bundled code, that comes in as an explicit contract term, never a default. Bump the engine version and add golden claims.
items.why: A billing person spots a 97010 allegation instantly: it is a false claim to a payer in the audit and a credibility-killing first impression in the free screening.
items.changes: Pricing engine: yes (the fee-schedule step; the closed list of unpriced reasons is unchanged). Ledger: no. Database: no. Freeze exception: yes.
items.lands_in: PR 6b (it already reopens this engine step under an approved exception), or PR 6c right after

items.title: Approved packets keep exporting figures after a correction or a withdrawn release
items.area: D30; ADR 0061; PR 5 export guard; PR 11
items.current: Once a line is in a case it keeps the priced line it had when the case opened. When a re-run is accepted (a CMS or contract correction) or a rule release is withdrawn because its content was wrong, an approved packet still passes approval, export and attestation, because those checks compare against the frozen case line. PR 5's withdrawal check covers only Medicare deadline windows, so a percent-of-Medicare contract line priced under a withdrawn release still exports. The screen says 'the case is judged again first', but nothing re-judges it until PR 11, which comes after PR 8 to PR 10 and relies on the daily monitor.
items.best: In PR 5 before it merges, add one database check, 'is this version's pricing still current': every line must still carry the pricing in effect, its release must not be withdrawn, and its contract version must still be signed off and cover the service date (this also catches a back-dated amendment). Enforce it at approval, export request, the export job, the export guard and attestation. Do not refuse to log a submission that already happened outside the product; flag it instead. Show the old and new expected figures and fix the copy. Add a triage reason so actionable totals drop on a withdrawal, and refuse an audit report built on a withdrawn release. In PR 11: accepting a re-run refreshes its cases in the same step; withdrawing a release queues every affected practice at once; packets already sent get an alert with a per-line difference so the practice can send the payer a correction; and a line whose re-pricing changes its pattern leaves the case with a coded reason.
items.why: Re-runs are routine (CMS publishes corrections every quarter), so today an approved packet can ask a payer for an amount PaidWhole already knows is wrong, which is exactly Gate 1's 'unsupported owed claim'.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no. Database: replaced bodies of existing check functions, written into PR 5's unmerged migration (you reconfirm the domain-model hash). Freeze exception: no.
items.lands_in: PR 5 before merge (the check, copy, triage reason); PR 11 (refresh on accept, withdrawal fan-out, sent-packet alert, pattern-change rule)

items.title: A 'verified' deadline can be later than the real one
items.area: D17; ADR 0061; engine dispute windows; Q34; D33
items.current: A contract dispute window can only be 'N calendar days from the payment date'. The specialist records the number of days and a quote, but not what the window runs from or whether the days are business days, so 'within 180 days of the date of service' is verified with a deadline weeks too late, and PR 5's export gate trusts it. Medicare Advantage non-contracted lines are verified from Original Medicare's redetermination window at level L2 (read by a person, not confirmed by the specialist), while question Q34 still asks whether that window applies at all; MA payment disputes actually run through each plan's own dispute policy. The synthetic L2 records state no start date.
items.best: In PR 5 before merge: the window citation also records its unit and what it runs from (date of service, remittance date, payment date, receipt), chosen from fixed lists and taken from the quote; 'verified' is refused unless the computed rule matches, and the abstraction screen shows the computed rule (for example 'ends 90 calendar days after the remittance date') beside the quote. Medicare Advantage non-contracted deadlines stay unverified until the specialist confirms the route (Q34); this means no MA packet exports until then. In PR 6c (freeze exception): the engine computes contract windows from the cited start and unit, and picks the MA route from the line's facts (payment dispute or reconsideration), each with its own record; after an upheld reconsideration the case waits for the independent reviewer instead of showing a provider deadline. In PR 8, with D33's dispute route: each plan's published dispute policy is cited on the MA mapping, and every dispute level uses one record shape. A contract that defers to the provider manual cites the manual's pages and revision date.
items.why: A deadline marked verified that falls after the real one is the worst failure this product can have: the billing manager files on the stated date, the payer refuses it as late, the money is gone, and 'verified' stops meaning anything.
items.changes: Pricing engine: yes, only the window calculation and the MA route lookup. Ledger: no. Database: new fields on the window evidence in PR 5, frozen at approval. Freeze exception: yes, for the engine part only. Expect MA actionable totals to drop until Q34 is answered.
items.lands_in: PR 5 before merge (guard, MA fail-closed); PR 6c (engine); PR 8 (MA plan policies, one route record per level)

items.title: The free screening can receive one patient's service line
items.current: A screening row may have a claim count of 1. A count-1 row with a calendar quarter, next to the practice's name and ZIP, is one patient's service line with a date finer than the year, which is not de-identified under HIPAA Safe Harbor. The prospect has no BAA, the screening tables are built and tested as non-PHI, and the public page promises 'no patient information'.
items.best: Require at least 11 claim lines per row (the CMS small-cell standard), as one setting enforced in the browser, in the server's check and in a database rule. The browser leaves small rows out before sending and tells the person how many rows, claim lines and dollars it left out, and the result says so too. A request that bypasses the browser is refused with row numbers. The template states the floor. Counsel confirms the number and whether it counts lines or patients (a plan of care can give one patient 11 lines in a quarter; if counsel says patients, add a patient-count column).
items.why: Your main lead channel would otherwise accept PHI from covered entities with no BAA into tables built as non-PHI: a privacy and legal failure that takes about a day to fix.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no. Database: one rule on the screening table, written into PR 6's own unmerged migration so it needs no extra approval round. Freeze exception: no.
items.lands_in: PR 6 before merge

items.title: The ledger compares payer approvals in allowed amounts and proof in cash
items.current: A payer 'approved' ledger entry is the increase in the allowed amount, while posted and deposited entries are cash. With 20% coinsurance, a $30.00 allowed increase pays $24.00: the line never reaches recovered and the ROI statement carries $6.00 'approved but not posted' forever. Worse, a line-level posting proves the gross payment rather than the payment net of the reversal it replaced, so recovered can include the patient's share, or money the payer never paid when a deductible absorbed the increase; and a later reversal takes back $30 against $24 posted. No ledger test has a patient share.
items.best: Keep deciding the outcome on the allowed amount (approved, confirmed, decreased, no change), as PRD 13 says, but measure every ledger amount in what the payer actually pays: 'approved' is the payer's payment increase on the line, a posting share is net of the reversal it replaced, and a reversal takes back what was paid. A correction a deductible absorbed is recorded with no entry and the case closes as 'payer corrected; balance is the patient's', never as recovered and never as no change. The allowed increase and the patient's share are shown beside it as 'billable to the patient', never counted. The definition of recovered, the proof cap and the seven entry types do not change. New ledger fixtures cover coinsurance, a deductible and a copay.
items.why: Recovered is the number buyers and firms audit first, and today it is wrong in both directions on every coinsurance line.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: yes, the amounts matching writes (you also settle PRD 13, which defines 'approved' two different ways). Database: no new columns; the figures come from stored line data. Freeze exception: yes.
items.lands_in: PR 15b beside PR 15; pull it earlier if ROI statements reach customers before PR 15

items.title: The payer's 835 that arrives after an EMR export is ignored
items.current: When a practice's EMR export of a payment loads first, the payer's own 835 for the same payment arrives later, is held, and nothing from it loads; the receipt says to open a support ticket. An export never carries provider-level adjustments, so a recoupment in that 835 (the repository's own test PAR-16 has a $75 one) never reaches the ledger: recovered is overstated and the seal can appear over money the payer took back. The bank deposit, which is the 835's payment net of those adjustments, can never match, and corrected claims never reach the adjusted-payments queue.
items.best: Keep the 835 authoritative and never replace priced lines silently (D13). When the 835 is held: add its provider-level adjustments to the export's remittance exactly once, with the 835 as evidence, so recoupments and interest flow through the ledger's unchanged rules; store the 835's net payment so the deposit matches; replace the support-ticket line with a code-computed comparison, claim by claim and line by line; hold any line where the 835 disagrees on allowed, paid or patient share, so no packet rests on figures the payer's own record contradicts; and link corrected claims. Then add a person-confirmed 'Replace with the payer's 835' action while nothing from the payment is in a case, ledger match or packet: the export's remittance is retired as a whole, the 835 loads, and a new pricing run prices it.
items.why: Loading the EMR export first is normal for EMR-export practices and for firms loading a backlog, and today a payer's clawback in the later 835 never reduces recovered, so the ROI statement and the seal overstate.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no rule changes; the entries arrive through existing rules. Database: new columns (evidence, net payment, a 'replaced' status) and one shared 'claims in effect' rule that every reader uses (domain model approval). Freeze exception: no.
items.lands_in: PR 4b for the adjustments, deposit, comparison and hold; PR 11 for the replace action

items.title: Claim-level copays create false underpayments
items.current: When a payer reports a copay only at claim level, the parser spreads it over the claim's lines by charge and triage judges each line alone. On a claim paid to the cent with a $40 copay, 97110 shows a $26.04 'shortfall'. Another legal 835 shape makes the parser count the copay twice, which shows false overpayments and hides real underpayments.
items.best: Fix the parser so the claim-level share is spread only over lines it actually reduced, and judge such claims as a whole against the claim's exact figures: the claim's lines validate at most the claim's net shortfall, nothing when it nets to zero, and a claim with an unpriced line goes to review. Store each case line's claimed amount so the case total, the packet and the ledger all use it. The packet schedule shows the claim-level share once and says the payer reported it at claim level.
items.why: It manufactures tens of dollars of shortfall on correctly paid claims at exactly the payers that report copays at claim level, and one disproven line discredits the whole packet.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: reads the new claimed amount. Database: one new column on case lines (domain model approval). Freeze exception: no.
items.lands_in: PR 6d, before PR 7

items.title: The multiple-procedure reduction is applied per claim, not per patient-day
items.current: The engine applies the multiple-procedure reduction within each claim, while Medicare applies it across all of one patient's claims for the day. A clinic that bills PT and OT on separate claims keeps one unit whole on each, so the expected amount is too high by roughly $6 to $15 per extra claim. The same gap lets a coding-edit (NCCI) pair split across two claims slip through.
items.best: Price a patient-day together: the worker groups one patient's claims in the run, the engine ranks the day's therapy units across them (by payee, payer, patient and date) and keeps exactly one whole, and the coding-edit check spans the same group. A primary and a secondary claim for the same services are never pooled. Triage caps pooled lines at the group's net shortfall, so a payer that kept a different unit whole raises no false allegation. No reads across runs are needed, because monthly runs already hold the whole day. Golden worksheet first.
items.why: Multi-discipline clinics usually bill each discipline on its own claim, so every such visit becomes a false Medicare Advantage allegation, and the pattern logic groups them into a case of false lines.
items.changes: Pricing engine: yes. Ledger: no. Database: no. Freeze exception: yes.
items.lands_in: PR 6c, sequenced with PR 6b so one engine version bump covers both

items.title: The insurer-payment figure and prompt-pay interest overstate what the payer owes
items.current: D31 plans the case's second figure as 'expected allowed minus the observed patient share, compared with paid'. That holds the patient's share fixed, so on a coinsurance line it charges the payer for the patient's coinsurance on the shortfall (in the worked example the payer owes $7.84 and D31 shows $9.80), and on most lines it simply repeats the headline. PR 5's prompt-pay interest is computed on the allowed shortfall, so the interest line in packets already built is too high by the patient's share.
items.best: Compute what the payer owes in code from the line's own cost sharing: a copay and a met deductible stay fixed, coinsurance scales at its observed rate, sequestration applies to the payer's part, one rounding. Where it cannot be known (the deductible took the whole line, the line was denied, the share was reported only at claim level), show a range from zero to the shortfall with the reason, never one number. Show the change in the patient's share as its own figure, never counted. Use the payer's figure, or the low end of the range, as the interest basis.
items.why: The interest line goes to the payer; overstating it on every coinsurance line makes the packet look careless and invites the reviewer to discount the rest.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no. Database: no. A packet format version bump for the interest section. Freeze exception: no. It must use the same basis as the sequestration fix (#2).
items.lands_in: Interest basis before the first real packet (with PR 6d); the full insurer figure in PR 13 with D31

items.title: Make your approval and the CI gate real
items.current: The domain-model approval is a line of text any session can type, and the approval of record was committed by the build agent. The agent works on GitHub as your own admin account, opening and merging pull requests. No branch is protected: PR #7 (PR 5's branch) went into main 51 seconds after it opened while CI was still running, and CI then failed; main, the default branch, now fails CO-02's own check, and Dependabot and scheduled jobs run against it. The protective hooks (approval line, fixtures, content releases) stay off until the final pass. Each approval asks you to re-read about 6,000 lines with no summary of what changed. The repository is public.
items.best: Give the build agent its own GitHub identity (a machine user or app with write but not admin rights) and take your admin token out of agent sessions. Protect main and the integration branch: required checks, branches up to date before merge, no force pushes, administrators included; then require your review on migrations, the domain model, content releases, CLAUDE.md and the .claude and .github folders. Until the agent has its own identity, sign each approval with your own SSH key (ideally a hardware key) and have CI verify the signature. Switch on the hooks now (hooks only; the push block and sandbox stay for the final pass). Open each approval with 'changes since the last approved document', with row-level security, the PHI registry and grants first. Make the integration branch the default (or point Dependabot at it), repair main, and consider making the repository private (branch protection on a private repository needs a paid GitHub plan).
items.why: CO-02 exists so you control the schema of a PHI system; today nothing shows you approved anything, and a failing change already reached the default branch, which is the first thing a SOC 2 auditor or an acquirer's diligence will find.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no. Database: no. GitHub settings (your clicks), the CI workflow, the approval check and a summary generator. Freeze exception: no.
items.lands_in: Governance PR now, before PR 5 and PR 6 are approved and merged

items.title: The Verified seal claims only what it proves
items.current: The ROI statement's seal reads 'Verified by PaidWhole / Reconciled to cash' when every line is at the practice's proof level, and that level defaults to 'posted'. Posting rows are usually auto-posted from the same ERA, so they are not evidence of cash; virtual-card payments post in full but deposit 2 to 5% less. The printed definition says expected amounts trace to signed-off contract versions, which is false for Medicare Advantage non-contracted lines. At posted level the statement says 'this practice supplies no deposit data' even when bank files were uploaded.
items.best: Award the seal and badge only at deposited proof, where every line is backed by a matched bank deposit; a posted statement carries no mark and says 'Recovered (posted): not yet matched to a bank deposit'. Use one always-true definition ('signed-off contract versions or the released Medicare fee schedule', in the brand owner's words) everywhere the mark appears. Make the posted wording true, and on the proof-level setting show the posted and deposited totals side by side once bank files exist.
items.why: The ROI statement is how an owner judges PaidWhole against its fees; if its one trust mark overclaims, every figure under it loses credibility. The trade-off: practices that cannot supply deposit data never earn the seal.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: an added refusal reason on the report (recovered, stages and matching unchanged). Database: no. You amend CO-11 and BRAND.md section 6, and the brand owner approves the words. Freeze exception: no.
items.lands_in: Small follow-up PR to PR 1, before PR 7's red team and before any ROI statement reaches a customer

items.title: The same payment under another trace number loads twice
items.current: An EMR export and an 835 count as the same payment only when their trace numbers match. ADR 0060 accepts that the same payment under another trace 'loads twice, the second for no review'. All four export layouts are guesses, so a 'Check #' column may hold a deposit or batch number, and Excel turns a 15-digit trace into 1.23457E+14. Two exports that name the payee differently also load twice. A double load doubles variance, cases and report totals, and since priced lines are permanent it cannot be undone.
items.best: At load, independent of the trace: when every claim of an incoming payment matches already-loaded claims of one other payment (claim number, patient account number, dates, charge and paid) and the amount agrees, hold it for review as 'same payment under another trace', linked to the earlier one; never drop it. A person can release it as a genuinely different payment, and that decision is recorded. Two 835s keep the existing reprocessing rules, so a payer's reprocessed claim still reaches the ledger. As a backstop, triage marks a line that repeats an open case line from another remittance, with no reversal between them, as not actionable, applied only to the non-authoritative copy so the real shortfall still counts once.
items.why: A doubled payment doubles every shortfall and sends the payer two disputes for one claim, and it cannot be undone once priced.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no. Database: a small practice-scoped table recording release decisions (domain model approval). Freeze exception: no.
items.lands_in: PR 4b, before PR 7

items.title: Excel-damaged files silently lose proof of recovery
items.current: Posting, bank and EMR exports are accepted as CSV only. A workbook is refused with 'Save it as CSV and upload it again', and that advice causes the damage: Excel writes long trace numbers as 1.23457E+15, drops leading zeros and rewrites dates and dollar formats. The readers accept any text as a trace, and a posting or bank row with an unreadable field is silently dropped while the screen says 'Read into rows and reconciled' with zero rows. Rows match remittances by exact trace text, so damaged traces never match, and a damaged EMR export loads beside its own 835.
items.best: First, quickly: record for every export how many rows were left out and why (column and row number, never values) and show it; refuse identifier cells written in scientific notation; change the advice to 'export again from your system; do not open and re-save it in Excel'; and accept '$1,234.56', accounting negatives and M/D/YYYY dates exactly. Then: when no exact trace matches, try the trace without leading zeros, but only with an exact amount match and never a partial one, and record how it matched. Then read .xlsx natively with a hardened reader built on the zip limits the contracts code already uses in production: dates from cell styles, amounts from their stored decimal text, numbers too long to be exact held for review.
items.why: Proof of recovery silently disappears in a routine billing workflow, so the recovered total and the ROI statement understate with nothing on screen saying why, and the export path can double a payment.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: readers gain additions, and matching gains the zero-tolerant fallback. Database: possibly a small table or report field for left-out rows. Freeze exception: yes, only for the trace-matching fallback, if you count matching rules as frozen.
items.lands_in: The quick part first (PR 4b's first commits, or a small PR now); the fallback and .xlsx in PR 4b, before PR 7

items.title: Unit cuts are invisible
items.current: The engine prices the units the payer paid, not the units billed (stored and never read), although the plan and the trace both say 'units as billed'. A payer that pays 3 of 4 billed units shows zero variance, the medically-unlikely-units check can never fire, a lesser-of contract compares mismatched figures and can invent a variance, and a fully cut line (0 paid units) crashes as an engine error that pages the operator.
items.best: Price the billed units. For claims with cut units, price a second time at the paid units through the unchanged engine (as the screening already prices twice), and split the variance exactly into a rate part and a units part. The rate part follows the normal rules; the units part is held for review until the treatment record supports the billed units (a reviewer can release it). Show the payer's reason code for the cut, label authorization cuts as such, and show billed and paid units side by side. Each export format states which units its column carries.
items.why: Unit cuts are a frequent therapy underpayment, and today they read as zero on every screen and in the Gate 1 audits.
items.changes: Pricing engine: methods unchanged (it is called twice, as the screening does). Ledger: no. Database: new columns on priced lines (domain model approval). Freeze exception: no.

items.title: Commercial reductions: allege only what the documents support
items.current: D32 holds a commercial shortfall explained by a reduction (for example the multiple-procedure reduction) for review when the rate record 'quotes no authority', but rate records never store a quote for their reduction flags. So every commercial case of this kind would be held forever, or the default 'off' would be read as authority. Contracts that pull in the payer's reimbursement policies by reference are not modeled, nothing says what ends a hold, and your confirmation of what CAS-22 means is not recorded.
items.best: For each reduction flag (multiple procedure, assistant, sequestration, NCCI), record its cited basis on the rate record once, at abstraction: a contract clause; an incorporated payer policy (the clause plus the policy document with its effective dates); the specialist's signed attestation that the contract is silent and incorporates nothing; or 'incorporation clause, policy not on file'. An incorporated policy that authorizes the reduction turns the flag on, so the engine prices it and nothing is alleged. Silence or an express exclusion makes the case actionable with a cited statement. A missing policy holds the case with 'obtain the payer's policy in force on these dates'. A payer policy that reduces differently from Medicare's method is shown, never alleged. Verifying refreshes the held lines at once, and Coverage shows 'waiting on authority review' by dollars and earliest deadline.
items.why: Commercial multiple-procedure reductions are one of the most specific findings this product makes; as planned they are either frozen in review or alleged against payers whose own policy allows them.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no (flags and defaults unchanged). Ledger: no. Database: added evidence fields and a new non-PHI document kind (domain model approval). Freeze exception: no. You confirm CAS-22's meaning in the PR 8 approval.
items.lands_in: PR 8 (records) and PR 9 (holds and gates)

items.title: Therapists not yet credentialed with the payer
items.current: Nothing records whether a therapist is credentialed with a payer. A new therapist's lines, paid out of network or denied, are priced at the in-network contract rate and become actionable. The rendering NPI is stored and never read, and rate records limited to a provider type can never price because the type is never passed in.
items.best: A participation record per payer and NPI, with dates, status and cited evidence, confirmed by a person from a roster the app builds from the remittances. 'Not participating' takes lines out of validated and actionable. Lines with credentialing denial codes go to review. A concentration check flags one NPI being short where colleagues are paid at contract, which catches the problem in the first audit with no data entry. 'No record' blocks only the payer-ready gate and shows on Coverage. Pass the provider type to the contract lookup.
items.why: In therapy groups the most common false underpayment is a therapist not yet credentialed; the payer rejects it, and the practice has sent an unsupported claim.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no (it supplies an input the lookup already defines). Ledger: no. Database: one new practice-scoped table (domain model approval). Freeze exception: no.
items.lands_in: New PR before the first real audit (after PR 6b), or the front of PR 8; the gate in PR 9

items.title: Name the payer's mistake in code
items.current: Triage names only two specific causes (a reduction not in the contract, last year's conversion factor); everything else is 'paid below the contract rate', and the detectors only work on percent-of-Medicare contracts. D34 deferred a model-written 'explain a variance' because the model gate is blocked on credentials.
items.best: Explain causes in code: each detector re-prices the line with the unchanged engine with exactly one thing changed, and must explain the payer's figure to the cent. Add: paid at the Medicare rate where the contract pays more; facility rate applied; sequestration not in the contract; assistant reduction without the modifier or not in the contract; last year's fee schedule; the superseded contract version (fixed schedules too, grouped by version so one missing amendment is one case); and another locality (only when the same locality explains several codes, and checked first against our own locality). Two causes that both fit are held as ambiguous. Reduction causes feed the authority review (#17). The payer's reason code is quoted as corroboration, never used to decide.
items.why: A packet that names exactly what the payer did ('paid the facility rate for place of service 11') is one system change for the payer to fix, while 'paid below the contract rate' invites a claim-by-claim review; different causes also stop sharing one case.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no (called, not changed). Ledger: no. Database: no. Freeze exception: no.
items.lands_in: PR 9 with the authority review; the cause shown on the case screen in PR 13

items.title: Small per-line shortfalls never become cases
items.current: A line counts as actionable only at a $5 shortfall. Systematic underpayments, such as last year's conversion factor (about 3.2%) or a schedule loaded a few percent low, come to 80 cents to about $5 a line, so 4,000 lines worth $8,000 show $0 actionable and never open a case. PRD 20 calls the $5 an estimate.
items.best: Judge materiality on the pattern: a line counts when its shortfall is more than payer rounding can explain (more than a cent per billed unit; lines a detector explains to the cent need only clear one cent), and the $250 case threshold stays the dollar gate. The per-line dollar threshold becomes an optional practice setting. Cases and packets show the line count, median shortfall and percent of expected, so approvers can spot an input error. The anomaly screen keeps its own $5.
items.why: In default settings, the patterns the product exists to find show $0 in every audit headline.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no. Database: no. You approve the PRD 12 and PRD 20 wording. Freeze exception: no.
items.lands_in: PR 6d (or PR 7)

items.title: Warn people before a dispute deadline passes
items.current: No deadline notification exists. The digest is monthly and counts deadlines within 14 days of the digest day, so a deadline on the 16th to the 31st never reaches anyone by email, and second-level deadlines after a denial are left out. The daily monitor silently writes off every line whose window has closed. The 'waiting on deadline verification' figure is one total that mixes passed windows with other blockers, the specialist queue does not list contracts whose window needs citing, and 'Request approval' notifies no one.
items.best: A daily alert ladder: at 30, 14, 7 and 2 days before a case's deadline, alert the owner (or every billing manager if it has no owner), add the approvers at 7 days if nothing is approved or exported, and the administrator at 2 days; stop once it is submitted. One daily roll-up email per person (counts, dollars, days left, one link; no dates or patient data). A morning notice when windows closed overnight. Alerts on unverified deadlines say the export is blocked and also reach the specialist queue, which lists the windows to cite sorted by earliest end. Split the waiting figure by cause. 'Request approval' notifies a chosen approver. The digest covers through the next digest, and the dashboard shows passed, 7, 14 and 30-day bands for cases not yet submitted.
items.why: One missed deadline loses a whole case's money for good, and the product itself writes the line off without a word.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no. Database: new notification kinds and preference keys (domain model approval). Freeze exception: no.
items.lands_in: Alerts PR right after PR 5 merges (the specialist-queue counts can go in PR 5); the approver choice in PR 14

items.title: Runs nobody triages, and re-pricing one click at a time
items.current: Only runs the monitor creates are triaged. A billing manager's own run prices and then nothing reaches Cases, and because the monitor now treats that month as covered, those lines never reach validated, a case or the digest while their windows run. Accepted re-runs are not triaged either. A correction or a withdrawn release must be re-run and accepted one run at a time, per month and per practice.
items.best: Triage after every run that takes effect: a person's first run when it completes, and a re-run when it is accepted (with the case refresh from #4). A daily job spots a newer release, a mapping correction or a back-dated contract sign-off, and creates re-runs only where lines actually change. One review page per practice shows a combined difference by cause and what it will set off (cases sent back for checking, sign-offs required), and accepts the selected re-runs in one action by their exact IDs. A withdrawal queues its re-runs automatically. The firm portfolio shows pending counts.
items.why: Validated shortfalls silently drop out of cases and digests today, and January and correction season turn into hundreds of clicks for firm analysts.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no. Database: one rule relaxed so a job may create a re-run after a withdrawal (domain model approval). Freeze exception: no.
items.lands_in: Triage after every run: now, before PR 7 (a few hours). Review page and withdrawal re-runs: PR 11 or a PR 11b right after. Firm counts: PR 17

items.title: One unmapped plan freezes a whole month
items.current: If any plan in a month has no mapping, the whole month's pricing run is refused and the monitor waits. A practice's first EMR export brings new plans, so every month it touches stops. Meanwhile the mapped payers' lines in that month go unpriced and their dispute windows run out unseen.
items.best: Price the month anyway: lines of an unmapped plan get the existing 'no mapping' reason and everything else prices. Warn before a manual run instead of refusing it. When the plan is mapped, create at most one re-run per affected month and let them be accepted together. The dashboard shows the dollars waiting and the earliest window among them. You decide whether a re-run that only prices the newly mapped lines takes effect without a separate acceptance.
items.why: Payers add plans all the time; one two-claim plan should not stop findings for every payer that month.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no. Database: no. Freeze exception: yes, because the milestone 3 check reads 'an unmapped plan blocks pricing'.
items.lands_in: PR 6c, before PR 7 so the red team attacks it

items.title: Multi-site groups are priced at one ZIP code
items.current: One ZIP per practice sets the Medicare locality for every line, although the plan treats locations as attributes of claims. North Carolina, the launch state, has one locality, so nothing is wrong today. In California, New York, Texas, Florida, Illinois, Pennsylvania or Missouri, a group with clinics in two localities gets every line priced at the billing office's locality: false allegations where the clinic's rate is higher, missed money where it is lower.
items.best: A dated register of each practice's sites (address ZIP and ZIP+4, the NPIs each site bills under, which therapists work where). Code decides each site's locality on each date; single-locality practices see no change. In a multi-locality practice each claim is assigned to a site by its payee NPI, then by rendering NPI only when that therapist works at one site; a claim no rule resolves is held, counted but carrying no dollars in any total, until someone assigns the NPI on Coverage. The unchanged engine gets the site's ZIP, and each priced line records which site and which rule were used.
items.why: Multi-site groups and their billing firms are the growth customers; this must be in place before onboarding any group outside a single-locality state.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no (it already takes a ZIP per claim). Ledger: no. Database: a new practice-scoped table and new columns on priced lines (domain model approval). Freeze exception: no.
items.lands_in: PR 6b stores ZIP+4 on the site record; resolution in a new PR right after PR 6b

items.title: Releasing packets: a reviewer queue now, a risk-based policy at scale
items.current: PR 5 makes every payer submission, at every practice, wait for PaidWhole's reimbursement reviewer (you, in v0) to open a four-hour support grant (which another internal person must create, and which notifies the practice administrator), download both files and attest. There is no queue across practices and no alert, so a packet can sit until its window closes and the monitor writes it off; practices can already download the files, so the gate mainly blocks logging the submission. The Medicare Advantage regulation confirmation is repeated for every packet version, and D29 counts every re-run as an 'override', so the yearly CMS update would send every case to extra sign-off.
items.best: Now, right after PR 5: a console reviewer queue across practices, sorted by deadline, with no patient data; the export job raises the access request automatically; reviewers get alerts, and the practice sees how long it has waited. In PR 14, after the payer-ready gates and D27: a review policy set from each practice's agreement. PaidWhole's attestation stays required for audit engagements, one-person practices, high-dollar, novel or overridden cases without a practice second signer, and practices that buy PaidWhole review; elsewhere a practice approver who did not draft it releases the packet, still downloading and hash-checking both files. Where review is required, the practice's own downloads wait for it too. A code-chosen sample of the other exports gets a non-blocking quality review that feeds the scorecard. 'Overridden' comes from what caused the re-run (mapping, contract, settings), not from a routine release update. The MA confirmation is kept per case and carried across versions until its citation, release or mapping changes.
items.why: As built, PaidWhole headcount caps how many packets every customer can send, firms cannot run their own disputes, and an approved packet can miss its window in a queue nobody sees.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no. Database: a practice setting, a reviewer notification kind, a console read function and permission rows (domain model approval). Freeze exception: no. Your download-before-attest ruling is kept wherever attestation applies.
items.lands_in: Reviewer queue: small PR right after PR 5 and PR 6b. Policy: PR 14, never before the single-user change (#35)

items.title: Export refusals are only written to a log
items.current: When PR 5's export job refuses a packet (case changed, deadline not verified, inputs differ, verifier failed), it only writes a log line and finishes as a success. The page said 'Reload in a moment', and after reloading it shows the same notice and the same Export button with no reason. The most common refusal comes when a line's window closes after approval, exactly when the billing manager is racing the rest. A job that crashes is equally invisible.
items.best: Check what can be checked before queuing (case unchanged, inputs current) and say no immediately with the remedy. Record every refusal or failure as a coded event with no patient data, and show the latest attempt on the packet page as in progress, refused with its fix, or failed. The payer-ready gates and invalidation refusals later use the same channel.
items.why: A billing manager working against a 90-day window clicks Export, sees nothing happen, and retries, files a ticket or misses the deadline.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no. Database: none now (audit events); an optional attempts table in PR 8. Freeze exception: no.
items.lands_in: PR 5 before merge; optional table in PR 8

items.title: Blind re-pricing that proves accuracy, and a benchmark buyers can reproduce
items.current: Gate 1 requires 200 lines independently re-priced with zero unsupported owed claims, and the change order promises 'a published benchmark'. Nothing in the product does either; the reviewer's attestation is one signature over the report, not a per-line, blind check.
items.best: Build a blind re-pricing check into the reviewer's report review, before release: a seeded random sample across all priced lines (more owed lines, plus some correctly paid and some unpriced), shown with the remittance facts and the contract documents but not the engine's choices or figure. The reviewer enters the amount and cites the clause; code compares to the cent and checks the cited page; release is refused while a sampled owed line is unsupported. Results feed the gates and the scorecard and add up to Gate 1's 200. Add a fixed root-cause code to 'payer correct on review' write-offs. Publish a benchmark on public CMS data only, reproducible by anyone, with each line labelled specialist-verified or worksheet-consistent; never publish agreement on synthetic fixtures as proof of accuracy.
items.why: It is the accuracy evidence for the funding gate and the answer to 'every EMR has a variance report'; done before release, it stops a wrong owed claim from reaching a customer.
items.changes: Pricing engine: read only. Ledger: no. Database: two new practice-scoped tables and an attestation field (domain model approval). Freeze exception: no.
items.lands_in: PR 7 (harness and definitions); PR 7b before the first real audit (the blind check); the public page after release 1 and the specialist's answers

items.title: One payer split in two between 835s and EMR exports
items.current: An EMR export names the payer and plans by text, while the 835 identifies them by ID, so one payer's shortfalls split into separate patterns that each must reach $250 alone (for example $180 and $150: neither opens a case). The mapping screen only lets an export plan use a contract of its own text-named payer, so the export months cannot be priced under the payer's existing contract without abstracting that contract a second time. Your 'No payer aliasing' ruling assumed the plans could be mapped to one contract, which the app refuses.
items.best: Let a person link payers and plans within a practice; code never links them by name. Suggestions come from evidence the loader already has (the same payment matched by claim numbers), with a name match only as a weak hint. Once a billing manager confirms (audited and reversible): the export plan uses the 835 plan's mapping, so there is no second contract; patterns, anomaly groups, digests, packets and the payer-ready check use the 835 payer; held patterns combine at the next triage; open cases keep their keys and a person decides any collision. A global payer directory (identifiers only) can come later for milestone 13.
items.why: Shortfall goes unpursued without anyone noticing, and a billing manager with both kinds of file cannot price a payer's export months at all without duplicating the contract.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no. Database: two new practice-scoped link tables (domain model approval). Freeze exception: no. Needs your new ruling refining 'No payer aliasing'.
items.lands_in: PR 4b (at the latest, the schema in PR 8 and the gate in PR 9)

items.title: EMR exports work only for four invented layouts
items.current: The EMR-export reader knows four vendor layouts, all invented placeholders; a real file whose headers differ is held whole until a vendor description arrives and a developer changes code. Posting exports can be mapped in the browser, EMR remittance exports cannot. One export is limited to 4 MiB (you kept that limit on 2026-10-18).
items.best: A per-practice column mapper that can add several columns into one field (deductible plus coinsurance plus copay) and refuses a column that is just a computed remainder. A preview runs the existing balance checks on the person's sample and flags a likely swapped patient-share column. In the worker, compare mapped lines with any matching 835: a layout becomes verified after enough lines agree, or after a second person checks sample lines against the EMR screen. Until then Coverage says 'not verified' and cases resting on those lines cannot export a payer packet (the same applies to the placeholder layouts). Verified layouts' headers can be shared with other practices. Optionally, if you reopen 'Both limits stand', a streaming reader lifts the 4 MiB limit.
items.why: As built, the export path cannot load a single real customer file, and a swapped column passes every balance check and produces false shortfalls in payer packets; only the comparison with the 835 catches it.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no. Database: a new practice-scoped layout table and a reference on documents (domain model approval). Freeze exception: no; the size part needs your ruling.
items.lands_in: PR 4b

items.title: Rehab-agency and hospital outpatient claims cannot be priced
items.current: A line billed on an institutional claim (rehab agency, CORF, hospital outpatient, Part B nursing facility or home health) has no place of service, so every percent-of-Medicare and Medicare Advantage line stops as an engine error and alerts the operator. On a mixed claim, a facility type of 22 or 23 can be misread as a place of service and priced at the lower facility rate.
items.best: Decide once per claim whether it is institutional. Add a cited rule record, through the release pipeline, that maps the bill type to Medicare's non-facility fee-schedule setting (CMS manual chapter 5); critical access and Maryland waiver hospitals stop with a named reason; a contract that names its own setting wins. The trace records the basis. The screening accepts a facility type in place of a place of service.
items.why: Many large multi-site PT groups bill as rehab agencies; today none of their Medicare-referenced lines can be priced, so the biggest accounts get the biggest coverage hole.
items.changes: Pricing engine: yes (a new input in the fee-schedule step and a new rule type). Ledger: no. Database: no. Freeze exception: yes.
items.lands_in: PR 6b's exception, or PR 6c right after

items.title: Price Original Medicare lines and use them to check our own accuracy
items.current: Original Medicare maps as 'government', which means no agreement: its lines are unpriced with the remedy 'None'. The free screening prices those same rows, so a prospect sees Medicare anomalies and then the paid audit shows them unpriced.
items.best: Add an Original Medicare mapping kind priced under the same Medicare terms, and treat it first as a benchmark: compare the engine's figure before sequestration with the Medicare contractor's allowed amount, leaving out lines with MIPS adjustments, and record the practice's Medicare participation status (non-participating providers are allowed 95%). A disagreement goes to the specialist, who attributes it to the contractor (then it is disputable under Medicare's own windows) or to us (a quality defect). Medicare Advantage packet lines export only when the same practice's Original Medicare lines agree for the same code, locality and quarter. Report the agreement as the scorecard's benchmark precision.
items.why: The Medicare contractor's payment is the closest thing to ground truth the engine will ever get, so every customer file becomes a continuous test that catches a wrong release before it turns into a false Medicare Advantage allegation.
items.changes: Pricing engine: yes (a new outcome; terms and arithmetic unchanged). Ledger: no. Database: the mapping-kind rule and a participation setting (domain model approval). Freeze exception: yes.
items.lands_in: PR 6b or PR 6c (outcome, participation); PR 7 (scorecard); PR 9 (export gate)

items.title: Work that starts before a case exists
items.current: Anomalies (a group of lines paid below its usual amount) have no owner, due date or clock, and are recreated for every pricing run. Unpriced lines carry no dispute window, so a commercial underpayment waiting on a contract loses its window with nothing on screen.
items.best: Keep D24 (no pre-case grades inside the case table) and add a lasting work item per payer, plan and fix (get the contract, map the plan, get the schedule, ask the specialist), with an owner, a next action, a checklist and a grade derived by code, carried across runs. Give it a clock computed from the default windows, labelled 'if your contract is silent; it may set an earlier date'. Coverage sorts these by dollars at risk, the digest warns 30 days out, and the item closes itself when the contract is signed off and the period re-priced.
items.why: A new practice usually has most of its contracts missing, and the windows keep running while the documents are gathered.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no. Database: a new practice-scoped table (domain model approval). Freeze exception: no.

items.title: One case status, and a closed state for a case that was paid
items.current: D25 adds a second status column using CO-06's vocabulary, which has no closed state for a case that was won and paid, and no path back for a second-level dispute. The two columns could disagree, four places already word case status differently, and readiness shows as codes.
items.best: One database routine writes both columns, with a rule that they can never disagree. Add a success closed state ('reconciled': every line not written off is recovered), which a recoupment reopens. Write the transition table into PR 8's domain model, including the loop to a second-level dispute and 'expired'. Use one 'is this case open' rule for every count, one shared wording for status everywhere (step plus outcome, such as 'Reopened by a recoupment'), and readiness in words with the failing gates named.
items.why: Every won case, the product's central outcome, would otherwise show as open forever in the billing manager's queue and the firm portfolio.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: read only. Database: rules on the case table (domain model approval; you approve the extra state). Freeze exception: no.
items.lands_in: PR 8 (vocabulary and rules), PR 10 (transitions), PR 13 (screens)

items.title: Every figure explained in words, and the drill-down guaranteed
items.current: The line trace page prints each calculation step as raw computer text, viewers see no steps, unpriced reasons show as bare codes, and the packet review screen and the packet PDF word the calculation differently. D5 (b) leaves open deferring the drill-down, the executive summary and the audit manifest, and PR 12's and PR 13's acceptance checks never test them or the executive and auditor export scopes.
items.best: One code-only renderer turns each line's stored trace into a plain sentence (for example '2 units x $50.00 = $100.00 under the contract's page 2 clause; rounded once; observed $70.00; short $30.00'), used on the line trace, the case Calculations tab, the packet review and the packet PDF, so the reviewer approves exactly what the payer reads. It says only what the trace records; a flag that is off is never worded as the contract's position. A test fails if any figure in a sentence is not in the trace or the rate record. Viewers get a version without dates. Close D5 (b) now, and add acceptance tests: a click path from case total to evidence, and each export scope's identifiers (the executive export carries none).
items.why: CFOs, billing managers and payer reviewers trust a number only when they can follow it, and today an executive export carrying member IDs would pass every planned check.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no. Database: no. Freeze exception: no.
items.lands_in: Renderer: small PR right after PR 5 merges; acceptance tests in PR 12 and PR 13

items.title: Owner-plus-biller practices are treated as one-person practices
items.current: A drafter can approve their own packet alone after 24 hours when nobody else in the practice holds approval rights. The owner (practice administrator or viewer) cannot hold approval rights, so the common owner-plus-biller practice counts as single-user and every packet routes to PaidWhole.
items.best: A free add-on 'packet approver' right that a person can hold on top of their existing role, so the owner approves in their own name and the practice gets ordinary two-person approval. For a truly one-person practice, record the drafter's act as the practice's authorization, not as the independent approval, which then comes only from PaidWhole's reviewer; drop the 24-hour wait. The approval card says 'Add approval to your owner's login, or send for PaidWhole review'.
items.why: Small PT practices are common, and sending every one of their packets to PaidWhole staff caps growth and puts you on every small customer's critical path.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no. Database: roles and the one-membership-per-organization rule (domain model approval). Freeze exception: no.
items.lands_in: PR 14

items.title: The worker process cannot act as a person
items.current: The web app and the background worker share one database login, and each declares who is acting. The worker is the most exposed process (it parses untrusted files and runs a browser to print packets), and a compromise there could forge an approval, a contract sign-off or an attestation in any practice's name. ADR 0061 defers closing this.
items.best: Give the worker its own database login and its own AWS role, which cannot read the web app's password. One database function then refuses any person's ID coming from a worker session, which covers every person-only step now and in future. A generated test runs each person-only step on the worker login and expects refusal.
items.why: It makes the attested-packet trust story unforgeable from the most exposed process, which enterprise security reviews probe first.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no. Database: a new login role and one tightened function (row-level security unchanged). Freeze exception: no.
items.lands_in: New PR just before PR 16, so the red team attacks it

items.title: Being signed out mid-narrative loses the work
items.current: PHI screens sign out after 30 minutes without a request to the server. Typing a packet narrative sends none, so on save the person lands on the sign-in page, the text is gone, and sign-in returns to the home page. There is no warning, and an unattended screen stays readable until the next click.
items.best: Typing and clicking count as activity (a quiet touch every 5 minutes while working), shared across tabs; a warning at 25 minutes with 'Stay signed in'; at 30 minutes the screen itself locks; after signing back in the person returns to where they were; and a notice before the 12-hour hard limit. Nothing is saved in the browser, and the limits themselves do not change.
items.why: Losing a carefully verified narrative is a trust failure people remember, and a PHI screen left readable past the idle limit fails a penetration test and the accessibility rule on time limits.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no. Database: no. Freeze exception: no.
