items.title: An outside auditor sees only the cases under review
items.current: D28 makes the auditor a practice-wide read-only role: an outside auditor would open every case in every practice of the group and could see patient names, although CO-06 says 'read-only on authorized cases' and D26's auditor export shows only a pseudonym.
items.best: A practice administrator shares named cases with a named auditor, with an end date and revocation. The auditor role gets no route into the practice at all, so a direct query returns nothing; reads go through checked functions that return pseudonymized case data and are logged in the practice's access log. The auditor works in the case screen's tabs, read-only, with the full drill-down, and creating the share generates the auditor-scope export.
items.why: HIPAA's minimum-necessary standard, and the compliance teams of groups and acquirers, will refuse practice-wide access for an outside reviewer.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no new rules on ledger or case tables. Database: two new practice-scoped tables and reviewed read functions (domain model approval; security review). Freeze exception: no.
items.lands_in: PR 14

items.title: A free screening a practice can finish: drop the 835 files
items.current: A prospect must build a pivot table by hand: one row per code, modifier set, units, place of service, payer product and quarter, with an allowed total and a claim count. Most practice owners and office managers cannot.
items.best: Let the prospect drop their own 835 files. A sandboxed worker in their browser, with no network access, parses them, removes duplicates, nets reversals, leaves out secondary-payer and denied lines, asks the person to choose the product for each payer and plan (never guessed), shows exactly which total rows will be sent, and sends only those through today's server checks. The minimum row size (#6) applies. EMR exports are added only once a format is confirmed. A follow-on sends each visit's combination of codes, so the unchanged engine prices the multiple-procedure reduction exactly instead of as a range.
items.why: Every billing manager can download 835s in a minute; almost none can build that pivot, and this is the top of the sales funnel.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no. Database: the screening tables change only for the visit follow-on (domain model approval). Freeze exception: no. You and counsel confirm that reading 835s only in the browser meets CO-04's 'no-PHI screening flow'.
items.lands_in: PR 6e, after PR 6b, before the screening opens with release 1

items.title: The screening says something about the commercial and MA contracted book
items.current: Commercial and Medicare Advantage contracted rows, most of a typical practice's dollars, only say 'N% cannot be priced without a contract'.
items.best: Keep them unpriced as expected amounts, but compute a Medicare reference for each (the fee-schedule amount for the units billed, before reductions and sequestration) and show 'Allowed as a percent of the Medicare fee schedule' by code and product, never 'below', 'expected' or 'owed'. Show it by payer only through a fixed payer directory (free-text payer names are never stored, since they can hold patient names). List quarter-to-quarter drops only per payer, with at least 30 lines a quarter. Define the ratio exactly as milestone 13's negotiation workspace will.
items.why: Percent of Medicare by code is the number owners negotiate with, so the screening says something useful about the part of the book they care about most, which raises conversion to a paid audit.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no. Database: screening tables and a global payer directory (domain model approval). Freeze exception: no. You approve the scope addition to CO-04 and D20.
items.lands_in: PR 6e

items.title: Screening results visible to the business, with consent
items.current: The only output of a screening is an emailed link to the prospect. Your console shows only the place-of-service split, a conversion carries no figure, and everything is deleted after 30 days, so you start the scoping call blind and cannot follow up.
items.best: An optional, unticked consent: 'PaidWhole may email me about this result and keep a summary of its totals for 12 months'. For consenting or converted prospects, keep a frozen summary of totals (with its release and the labels from your rulings); a console list shows those leads only, and other screenings only as counts; converted requests show 'From a screening' and the summary; consenting prospects get a reminder before deletion; and the scorecard gets screening-to-audit conversion.
items.why: You walk into the scoping call knowing the prospect's Medicare Advantage exposure, and the channel the change order leads with becomes measurable.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no. Database: screening tables (domain model approval). Freeze exception: no. Keeping a summary past 30 days is a CO-04 amendment you approve, and the prospect-facing wording changes.
items.lands_in: PR 6e, before the screening opens; the conversion measures in PR 7's scorecard

items.title: Fee schedule exhibits entered in minutes, not hundreds of forms
items.current: A fixed fee schedule has one amount per rate record, so a 150-code exhibit becomes 150 records with 5 approvals each: about 750 page reloads plus hand entry. The model-proposal path fails on schedules that size because its answer is cut off.
items.best: A code-only importer: keep each spreadsheet or CSV row's cells in position at intake; the specialist maps the header (code, modifiers, place, amount, dates) once; code reads every row exactly, lists every exception (never rounds, never skips silently), refuses duplicates, flags amounts far from the Medicare amount for the same code, and builds draft records citing the row. A keyboard review table approves a row's fields in one step. For PDF exhibits, ask the model one page range at a time.
items.why: Specialist hours per contract decide how many practices can onboard each month, and code-read amounts are more accurate than 150 retyped ones.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no. Database: no. Freeze exception: no.
items.lands_in: New PR after PR 6b, before PR 7 (before design-partner contracts arrive)

items.title: Firm clients onboard without a founder call
items.current: A firm can invite only practices already on PaidWhole. Every new practice goes through your scoping call and a console setup by hand, and a converted screening also lands in that queue.
items.best: A firm sends an invitation (one at a time or by CSV, with the NPI and last four of the TIN only); no workspace exists until the invited person accepts. That person enrolls MFA, creates their own group and practice, e-signs the BAA, data-rights addendum and engagement, and approves the firm's grant, so the practice still owns its workspace. Guards: the invitee may not be a member of the firm or on its email domain (a new check on grant approval), the NPI is checked against the public NPPES registry, and an NPI already on PaidWhole is never duplicated. When every check passes the practice opens at once; otherwise it waits in a console queue with uploads closed. There is no payment step when the firm pays.
items.why: A firm with 30 clients needs 30 of your calls today, which caps 'practices per firm login' and 'hours to onboard' at your calendar.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no. Database: an invitation variant, a tighter grant-approval rule and an activation state (domain model approval; security review). Freeze exception: no.
items.lands_in: PR 17; direct self-serve from a screening in a new PR after PR 17

items.title: The firm's working surface: full portfolio, deadline queue, grant renewals
items.current: PR 17 builds CO-08's minimal portfolio. The rest of the plan's portfolio (freshness, review queue, actionable and recovered kept apart, sorting, grant expiry, extension requests) is scheduled nowhere. Grants last 12 months with no warning before they end, so a firm can lose access mid-dispute, and an analyst with 40 clients switches between 40 workspaces to see what is due.
items.best: Full practice cards; a cross-practice deadline queue of case rows with no patient fields (from a fixed list of columns), sorted by deadline, with bulk assign that checks each case; one inbox across practices; grant-end notices at 60, 30 and 7 days, a flag when a grant ends before an open case's deadline, and a renewal request the practice approves as a new grant; and 'needs an owner' derived for every cause, not only revocation. Milestone 12 adds the firm ROI per practice and in total, and a payer view for prioritizing (packets stay per practice).
items.why: Missed deadlines and analyst minutes grow with every client, and a grant that lapses silently loses access in the middle of a dispute (and stops billing).
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no. Database: notification kinds, a grant-extension request table and a permission for analysts (domain model approval). Freeze exception: no. You amend CO-08's 'counts and dollars only' wording to allow case rows with no patient data.
items.lands_in: PR 17; the firm ROI and payer view in milestone 12

items.title: A time log so pursuit cost and hours saved are real
items.current: The ROI statement prints 'Pursuit hours logged: 0.00' because no milestone builds a time log. Gate 2's 'analyst hours saved against the firm's baseline' and two scorecard measures cannot be computed.
items.best: An append-only time log entered at the moments work is already recorded (exporting, submitting, recording a response, a follow-up), prefilled from the practice's defaults, plus 'Log time' for calls and portals; an optional timer that only suggests; no passive tracking of staff. Actual cost shows beside the original estimate, which never changes. The ROI statement fills its existing hours field and says how many cases have time logged. The firm's baseline is a dated record of who set it and how.
items.why: Firms buy on analyst time saved, and Gate 2 cannot be passed or even measured without it.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no (the hours field already exists). Database: one new practice-scoped table (domain model approval). Freeze exception: no.
items.lands_in: PR 8 (table), PR 13 (screens), PR 17 (baseline); PR 7 marks the measures as missing until then

items.title: Billing that follows customer size and gets firm-paid practices right
items.current: There is one flat subscription per organization: a group with 12 practices pays the same as one with a single practice. Firms are billed per granted practice from counts only, and nothing records who pays for a firm's client, so a firm-paid practice's ROI statement shows $0 fees and no ratio, and a firm that stops paying keeps working on its clients. Every audit invoice is the catalog price whatever the scope.
items.best: Keep a record of who pays for each practice on each day (proposed by the firm in its invitation, accepted by the practice, ended by either side from a date). Record per-practice daily usage with opaque IDs only; send firm invoices with one line per practice; attribute fees so each ROI statement is right (the firm decides whether its price is shown to its client). Refuse new work by a suspended firm's users on its grants; tell the practice and give it a grace period and a one-step takeover. Price group subscriptions per practice. Let the audit invoice take the scoped amount from the engagement letter.
items.why: Under a flat fee the largest groups are the least profitable, and the ROI statements firms use to sell PaidWhole to their clients show no fees.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: read only. Database: billing tables and a reviewed function that returns opaque IDs (domain model approval; security review). Freeze exception: no.
items.lands_in: PR 17 (who pays, consent); milestone 12 (invoicing, per-practice price, refusal)

items.title: Remittances that arrive by themselves, and knowing when one is missing
items.current: Every 835, EMR export, posting export and bank file is uploaded by hand. The dashboard shows the last file but not whether a payer's remittances have stopped arriving, and nothing tells the payer-ready gate whether a newer remittance is missing, so a packet could ask for money that a later, un-uploaded remittance already paid.
items.best: First, per-payer freshness computed from each payer's usual cadence, on the dashboard, portfolio and digest, and fed into the payer-ready gate: a case cannot become payer-ready until newer files are uploaded or a person records there are none. Then a copies-only delivery channel: a per-practice secure drop (AWS Transfer Family, keys only) where the clearinghouse sends copies of 835s and the PM system and bank send posting and deposit files. Files get generated names (the sender's filename, which can carry patient data, is never kept), go through the existing scanned intake and duplicate rules, and a firm's shared channel routes only to practices that registered that payee. Clearinghouses are then added one at a time through their official delivery; PaidWhole never holds a portal login, which could submit claims or change ERA routing.
items.why: A monitoring subscription fed by a monthly manual chore loses data, then findings, then renewals, and automatic bank files make 'deposited', the seal's proof, the normal case.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no. Database: new practice-scoped channel tables, and a change to the document uploader rule so a delivered file has a lawful uploader (a row-level security change; security review). Freeze exception: yes, for that rule. Adding a new PR needs your agreement under D5.
items.lands_in: Freshness and gate: PR 9 and the dashboard. Secure drop: a new PR beside milestone 12. Connectors: per partner, after the design-partner interviews

items.title: Screens that stay fast as history grows
items.current: Every dashboard, Coverage, Contracts and report view works out 'which pricing is in effect' again from every priced line the practice has ever had. A mid-size practice with three years of history has about 288,000 priced lines, about half a second per query and four or more queries per dashboard, growing with every month and every re-run; a firm portfolio across 50 clients would take tens of seconds.
items.best: Keep a pointer table of the pricing in effect, written at the only two moments it changes (a first run completes; a re-run is accepted, which must take the same lock), and a coverage snapshot written at the same moments. Stage figures, deadlines and short dollars stay live, but run over the narrow tables. Add a parity test and a nightly check against the current method, and a speed budget in CI.
items.why: Firms will judge the product on its most-viewed screens, and the shared database would saturate as history grows.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no. Database: two new practice-scoped tables (the pricing tables themselves are unchanged; domain model approval). Freeze exception: no.
items.lands_in: New PR just before PR 17, or the start of PR 17

items.title: The packet cover identifies the provider the way payers file disputes
items.current: A dispute packet's 'From' line is the practice name, one NPI and 'tax ID ending ####'. The loader drops the payee's name, TIN and address from every 835, and the payer-ready check for the right legal entity has no remittance-side TIN to compare.
items.best: Keep the payee's name, TIN (sealed) and address from the 835. Confirm the practice's legal entity and full TIN only when they match a loaded remittance. The payer-ready check compares the remittance payee with the contract's legal entity (D33). The cover prints the legal entity, the NPIs and TIN from the disputed remittances, a correspondence address and phone, the approver as contact, and 'prepared by <firm> on behalf of <practice>' under a firm grant; the TIN is masked in the auditor and executive scopes.
items.why: Payers file disputes against TIN plus NPI and reply to an address; a cover that lacks them is easy to return as incomplete inside the dispute window.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no. Database: new columns on remittance and practice (domain model approval). Freeze exception: no.
items.lands_in: PR 8 and PR 9 (records and check); PR 12 (cover)

items.title: Export-loaded claims are missing the patient name and member ID
items.current: No EMR export layout carries a patient name or member ID, so every export-loaded line in a packet prints 'not on the remittance' in those columns, and export patients never join their 835 records.
items.best: Add optional name and member-ID fields to the layouts; key a patient as the 835 path does only when a member ID is present; when a held 835 matches, copy its names and member IDs onto the export claims (fill blanks only; list disagreements). At payer export, a readiness check names the rows lacking them and the remedy, and the approver can still send with an acknowledgement rather than a hard refusal.
items.why: Payer dispute units identify claims by member ID and name, and a schedule full of 'not on the remittance' risks being returned inside the window.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no. Database: no new table. Freeze exception: no.
items.lands_in: PR 4b (fields and identity fill); PR 12 (readiness check)

items.title: A status page outside the app, and recovery from a regional outage
items.current: The public status page is served by the same app and database, so it goes down with them, and staff must update it through the console that is also down. Production runs in one AWS region with no cross-region copies and no stated recovery time, and the practices' data keys sit under a single-region key that AWS cannot convert later.
items.best: Before the first production deploy, create the environment key as a multi-region key (this cannot be added later without re-encrypting everything). Then replicate database backups and the document buckets to a second US region, state recovery-time and data-loss targets in a contingency plan mapped to HIPAA, and drill a regional restore every year. Use a hosted status service outside PaidWhole's account (no PHI on it), fed automatically by the uptime checks and the worker heartbeat, with email and webhook subscriptions and 90 days of history.
items.why: Firm and group security questionnaires ask for uptime history and disaster recovery, and today a regional outage has no recovery path for practices in the middle of a deadline.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no. Database: a region column on the restore-drill record (domain model approval). Freeze exception: no.
items.lands_in: New infrastructure PR before the first production deploy

items.title: A contract calendar with cited notice terms that rolls forward
items.current: The contract's notice period is stored as an uncited number of days. The calendar assumes every contract renews yearly on its start date, and its events are computed once at sign-off and never again, so after the first notice deadline an open-ended contract's calendar goes blank. The digest counts only contracts with an end date, so the usual auto-renewing contract reports zero.
items.best: Cite the term, renewal and notice clauses (verified by the specialist, frozen like the dispute window), compute upcoming anniversaries and notice deadlines on read so they roll forward each year, and have the digest count notice deadlines, open-ended contracts included. Milestone 13 alerts at 120, 60, 30 and 7 days, linking to the negotiation workspace.
items.why: Payer contracts often auto-renew and need 90 to 180 days' notice, and a calendar that goes blank in year two is trusted exactly when it is wrong.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no. Database: new fields on contract versions (domain model approval). Freeze exception: no.
items.lands_in: PR 8 (citations, rolling calendar, digest); milestone 13 (alerts)

items.title: Contract escalators
items.current: There is no escalator term ('increases 3% each anniversary'). The workaround needs a person to compute each year's factor, which rule 1 forbids, and on a lesser-of contract it produces a wrong number; an open-ended base record silently keeps pricing year two at the base rate, so the shortfall reads zero.
items.best: An escalator parameter with its own citation (percent, cadence, anchor, compounding), applied by the engine before the lesser-of comparison, with one rounding. The abstraction screen requires 'escalation clause: none, modelled or index-linked' before sign-off; CPI-linked escalators stay unsupported rather than guessed. Refuse the wrong-number workaround in the meantime.
items.why: Payers that fail to load escalators and keep paying the base-year rate are a classic underpayment pattern the product would otherwise miss entirely.
items.changes: Pricing engine: yes (a new method parameter). Ledger: no. Database: no. Freeze exception: yes.
items.lands_in: PR 6c

items.title: Mutation testing that actually runs on the money code
items.current: Mutation testing (a check that the tests would catch a deliberate bug) has a CI job that can never run on schedule, and its runner reports results without running the tests. Only the packet verifier has a measured score; the plan requires 85% on the engine and the ledger.
items.best: Check which runner reports truthfully, give the engine, the ledger and the verifier their own configurations, run on changed files in each pull request and in full every night, fail below 85% per package, keep a reviewed list of surviving mutants in the money arithmetic, and make it an exit condition of milestone 6 and Gate 1.
items.why: Until the specialist's golden answers arrive, this is the strongest independent evidence that the tests really pin the arithmetic behind every dollar.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no (tests only). Ledger: no (tests only). Database: no. Freeze exception: no.
items.lands_in: PR 7 (or the governance PR)

items.title: The red team keeps every case it writes
items.current: The milestone 6 red team keeps only tests that reproduce a defect, in a quarantined suite outside CI, and the defect list is a markdown file someone reads. The agent cannot actually register a fixture, and nothing says where its expected answers come from.
items.best: Keep every adversarial case as a permanent synthetic case checked by the external 835 validator; take expected amounts from the independent worksheet or a cited rule, never from the system under test; run the quarantine in CI so a fixed-but-still-quarantined defect turns it red; keep the defect list as data that a gate check reads; and run the agent on the most capable model.
items.why: A red team whose expected answers are copied from the code cannot find money defects, and passed cases that are thrown away let old faults come back unseen.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no. Database: no. Freeze exception: no.
items.lands_in: PR 7; the same rules in PR 16

items.title: Payer submission layouts for bulk disputes
items.current: PR 12 plans one CSV line schedule for every payer, though CO-06 allows XLSX. Payers' bulk-dispute channels often require their own template, so analysts retype hundreds of lines, and the file sent is no longer the file that was hashed and attested.
items.best: A registry of payer submission layouts per dispute route (D33), each column drawn from a fixed list of packet fields; a layout that needs a field the packet lacks, or one outside the payer scope, is refused for that packet. A deterministic XLSX writer produces the layout, reads it back to check every cell and splits files over the row limit, and the reviewer downloads and hash-checks each file before attesting.
items.why: Retyping undoes the verifier and the hash chain and costs analyst minutes on every case.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no. Database: two columns on PR 8's export-part table. Freeze exception: no.
items.lands_in: PR 12 (columns in PR 8)

items.title: A capacity baseline and backlog alarms
items.current: Production runs one small worker task that handles every job type one at a time, with no autoscaling and no alarm when work backs up. Intake waits up to 10 minutes for the malware scan while holding its slot, printing shares memory with pricing, the screening queue sits behind other platform jobs, the worker has half the CPU the plan's own speed target assumes, and the database has no storage or memory alarms.
items.best: A backlog metric and alarms per queue against stated targets; intake re-queues itself instead of waiting during the scan; fair per-practice concurrency for pricing, triage and reconciliation; size the worker to the plan's own figure and move printing to its own service; autoscale on backlog age; add database alarms and a runbook threshold for a bigger class; and run a staging load test at three times the Gate 1 target before Gate 1 and milestone 12. No read replica or connection proxy until there is a measured need.
items.why: A slow backlog is invisible today, and month-start uploads at scale would leave billing managers waiting hours for findings.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no. Database: no schema change. Freeze exception: no.
items.lands_in: New PR after PR 17, before Gate 1 and milestone 12

items.title: Task-bound access for contract specialists
items.current: Each contract specialist session needs a four-hour support grant, created by a second internal person and announced to the practice administrator, and during it the database exposes every PHI table of that practice, narrowed only by the app. PR 5 adds window citation for every contract to the same queue.
items.best: A contract-review access opened by the practice's own upload or request, while a practice setting allows it, and closed at sign-off or after 14 idle days. The specialist claims the item without a second person. The database admits only the contract tables and the contract documents named by that item, so every other PHI table refuses by default. One notice per review, and every read logged. Payer letters, ledger adjustments and attestation stay on the break-glass support grant.
items.why: Specialist throughput limits onboarding, and the narrower scope exposes less patient data than today's support path.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no. Database: a new scope setting and policies (a row-level security change; security review). Freeze exception: yes. It amends ADR 0019, ADR 0028 and PRD 3.
items.lands_in: PR 14

items.title: Claims and lines: payer, reasons in words, filters that reach the remedy
items.current: The Claims and lines table has no payer column (the query already returns it), shows unpriced reasons as bare codes, has no sort or export, and cannot filter to unpriced lines or to a reason, so the Coverage screen's remedy link lands on every line.
items.best: Show payer and plan, unpriced reasons in words with their remedy, an Unpriced filter and a reason filter that Coverage links to, and sorts by largest shortfall, date and payer. Add a logged line export for PHI roles as a background job in milestone 12, and a volume test on a million synthetic lines before adding any index.
items.why: This is the billing manager's working table, and today the 12 lines that need review cannot be found among thousands.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no. Database: none unless the volume test needs a column (then domain model approval). Freeze exception: no.
items.lands_in: Small PR after PR 6b; the export in milestone 12; the volume work in the final pass

items.title: Bulk mapping and bulk case work
items.current: Mapping offers one 'Map this plan' page per plan (50 to 150 at onboarding), case lines are written off one at a time, there is no bulk assign, and on the Cases screen the case list sits below three setup panels.
items.best: Map many plans of one payer to one signed-off version in one step, with a per-plan preview of what will price and what falls outside the dates; never preselect a version, and hold Medicare Advantage or out-of-network plans out unless ticked. Select case lines across pages and write off or reopen them under one reason, with the count and total shown. Put the case list first. Add bulk assign with D36's 'needs an owner' list. Each item keeps its own audit event.
items.why: When a payer answers 'correct on review' for 120 lines, today that is 120 separate forms.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no. Database: no. Freeze exception: no.
items.lands_in: Mapping in bulk: a small new PR; case lines and layout: PR 13; bulk assign: PR 17

items.title: Packet builder: no dead Approve button, one form, accessibility everywhere
items.current: The drafter sees a working Approve button that the database then refuses. The packet's prompt-pay and evidence fields appear three times with the same IDs, and a choice made in one copy is silently dropped when another button submits (the interest line can disappear). Accessibility checks skip the packet builder and most core screens.
items.best: Show the drafter a disabled button with the reason, next to 'Request approval'; use one form with one set of fields and three submit buttons, with unique IDs. Run the accessibility check automatically after every page and form in every test journey, and fail the run if a screen in the route list was never checked.
items.why: A button that always fails says the product is broken, the dropped interest choice understates the claim, and health-system buyers check accessibility.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no. Database: no. Freeze exception: no.
items.lands_in: PR 5 before merge (the page); PR 7 (the accessibility gate)

items.title: Getting to your first finding
items.current: Settings has a 'Getting started' list that ends at the first upload and that only administrators see. Nothing shows the rest of the path to a first finding (contracts tagged, abstraction, sign-off, mapping, first run, triage) or who each step waits on.
items.best: One live 'Getting to your first finding' card on the dashboard, computed from existing records, with each step naming who acts (the practice, the specialist, PaidWhole) and a link. It completes when the first run is triaged, reporting what was found, not when a case opens. The same step times feed the scorecard's onboarding measures.
items.why: A new administrator does not know that the contract they never uploaded is why nothing is priced.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no. Database: no. Freeze exception: no.
items.lands_in: Inside PR 7 beside the scorecard, or a small PR after it

items.title: Single sign-on for firms and groups
items.current: Sign-in is Cognito with MFA, and single sign-on waits for the first firm's security review; ADR 0055 wrongly says it would force a change of identity vendor.
items.best: Per-organization SAML or OIDC sign-on on the same Cognito pool, with verified domains, invitation-only first sign-in, MFA asserted by the customer's identity provider or an in-app passkey step, enforcement that closes the password route for that domain, deprovisioning through SCIM so a disabled user is signed out on the next request, and an audit export.
items.why: Firms and PE-backed groups require SSO in procurement, and offboarded staff otherwise keep app accounts until someone removes them by hand.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no. Database: new non-PHI configuration tables (domain model approval). Freeze exception: no.
items.lands_in: Milestone 12

items.title: Show customers that disputed patterns stay fixed
items.current: Nothing measures whether a payer keeps paying a disputed pattern correctly after the dispute; only cash recovered is counted, and it falls in year two, when renewal is decided.
items.best: A separately labelled measure, never added to any stage or called recovered: for lines of the same payer, plan and agreement exposed to the same cause and paid after the first submission (by payment date), how many are paid at contract and how many are still short, and the per-line shortfall before and after; the case's own lines are excluded. Store it as a written-once snapshot and show it on the case, on a separate page of the ROI statement and in the firm roll-up, in observational wording.
items.why: It proves ongoing value with numbers the engine computed, which supports gross retention, one of the change order's moat measures.
items.changes: Pricing engine: no. Ledger: no. Database: a new practice-scoped snapshot table (domain model approval). Freeze exception: no.
